Hi Sofia —

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. We ran a quick internal sanity check against our colo network policy and wanted to make sure Redwood’s sizing assumptions line up with what we can actually provision. High-level notes: 

- Peak concurrent requests: estimated 1.2k concurrent chats (95th) with average prompt+response token window ~450 tokens.
- Expected steady-state RPS (inference requests): ~150 rps, but spikes to 700 rps for up to 10 minutes (daily backup window).
- Egress limits from our rack: 4 Gbps sustained per cluster, 8 Gbps burst for <5 min.

Could you confirm whether the default private pool config you shared (8xA100-80GB per pod, 3 pods in pool with continuous batching) will meet the 95th percentile latency target of 300ms p50 / 600ms p95 given those network caps? Also attaching our network policy matrix (network-egress-matrix.pdf) and a stubbed sizing spreadsheet.

Appreciate a quick sanity check — we’re on a tight timeline for staging next week.

— Alex

Sofia / team — ran a short simulation on the sizing model (attached: redwood-sizing-model-v3.xlsx). Summary: 

- Baseline config tested: 3 pods x 8xA100-80GB, continuous-batch size target 32 (token-aware batching), KV cache enabled.
- Steady 150 rps: p50 120ms, p95 280ms, p99 470ms. Network egress utilization ~1.1 Gbps.
- 700 rps 10-minute spike (no autoscale): p50 310ms, p95 730ms, p99 1.4s. Egress Utilization ~3.8 Gbps (close to your sustained cap).
- Autoscale policy simulated: add +2 pods when 1-min p95 > 600ms OR CPU sustained > 75% for 60s. With autoscale, during spike p95 falls to 420ms after ~70s (including pod spin-up and model warm).

Observations / recommendations: 
- Given the 4 Gbps sustained egress cap, the static 3-pod config will be okay for steady traffic but will exceed latency SLOs during long spikes without autoscale.
- We can reduce burst impact by: 
  - enabling KV prefix caching for common prompts (reduces model compute + tokens sent),
  - pre-warming a lightweight model shard (quantized) to answer the top ~20% of requests (degrades some quality but saves egress),
  - tightening default batch window to prioritize latency (batch window 15ms -> target batch size falls, but p95 improves ~100–150ms).

I uploaded detailed sim graphs into the Drive link in the thread. Attaching the sizing workbook.

— Dev
Senior Inference Engineer, Redwood Inference

Good notes — adding networking specifics and operational constraints. Two items from my side: 

1) Network egress shaping: if Meridian cannot raise the sustained cap above 4 Gbps, we should set an explicit egress-aware routing policy. Implementation sketch: mark requests with large expected response token counts and route them to a secondary quantized pool that has lower output size. This keeps the primary pool responsive for short/medium responses.

2) Failure modes & degraded behavior: we must document expected degradation paths so support teams can communicate to the customer. Proposed bullets for runbook: 
  - If sustained egress >= 3.8 Gbps for >5m, automatically shift 30% of requests with detected long-response templates to the quantized fallback pool.
  - If autoscale cannot provision extra pods within 150s, enable immediate short-response mode (truncate responses at 300 tokens) and activate a lightweight Rerank+Shorten hook.

3) Network warmup: encourage Meridian to permit a small continuous background traffic (1–2 rps) that exercises the KV cache for top 100 prompt families for 24h prior to cutover. This reduces cold-start egress during ramp.

I updated deployment-checklist-v1.md with these items and linked it in Drive.

— Marcus
Principal Reliability Engineer, Redwood Inference

- To respect your 4 Gbps cap we recommend a combination of autoscale + egress-aware routing + pre-warm cache.
